areas.name: Thompson Peak
areas.blurb: Thompson Peak is the highest summit in Idaho's Sawtooth Range, a granite high point rising above the Redfish Lake area near Stanley in the Sawtooth Wilderness. Its standard route is a long but non-technical day, with trail, off-trail travel past a high alpine lake and only a short Class 3 finish.

routes.name: East Ridge
routes.rock_grade: Sustained Class 3 on the upper ridge crest
routes.best_season: Mid-summer to early fall, once the ridge is snow-free and the rough road has dried out. Early-season snow lingers on the upper ridge, and fall storms can coat the rock in snow and ice.
routes.overview: The East Ridge is the standard way up Diamond Peak, the highest summit in the Lemhi Range and one of Idaho's few ultra-prominent peaks. From a high trailhead reached by a rough dirt road, a short, steep climbers' path leads onto a long ridge that rises about 3,000 ft from treeline to the top. The upper half is a sustained Class 3 scramble with big views over the Birch Creek Valley far below.
routes.beta: From the parking area, follow the remains of an old jeep track and then a worn climbers' path up grassy slopes to a saddle on the ridge at about 9,300-9,400 ft. Climb steeply up the ridge to around 10,200 ft, where it bends northwest, and continue up to about 10,800 ft. From here the ridge narrows and the scrambling becomes sustained: a series of short rock steps, roughly 10-30 ft high, around 11,000 ft form the crux, followed by long stretches of easier Class 2-3 scrambling to the summit. Stay on or very close to the crest, dropping just left of it when needed; the faces on either side quickly turn into Class 4-5 terrain.
routes.approach: From Idaho Highway 28 in the Birch Creek Valley on the east side of the Lemhi Range, turn west on the signed Pass Creek Road (north of the old Blue Dome site). Beyond the first couple of miles the road fords Pass Creek and becomes rough; stay on the main track through a gate and into the national forest. The road finishes as rough jeep tracks to a small saddle with a fire ring at about 8,000 ft, where parties park.
routes.descent_text: Descend the same way along the East Ridge, staying on the crest through the Class 3 steps, then follow the climbers' path back down the grassy slopes to the parking area.
routes.turnaround: Turn back if you have not reached the start of the sustained scrambling around 10,800 ft by late morning, or if storms are building over the range.
routes.bail: Retreat is back down the ridge the way you came; do not try to shortcut off either side of the crest, which quickly becomes cliffy Class 4-5 terrain.

pitch_detail.notes: Old jeep track and worn climbers' path up grassy slopes from about 8,000 ft to a saddle near 9,300-9,400 ft.
Steep ridge climbing to about 10,200 ft, where the ridge bends northwest, then on to about 10,800 ft.
A series of short rock steps, roughly 10-30 ft high, around 11,000 ft. Stay close to the crest.
Long stretch of mixed Class 2 and 3 scrambling on or just left of the crest to the summit at 12,197 ft.

what_to_bring: Plenty of water - there is none on the ridge
Map and navigation for the ridge
Spare tire and recovery gear for the road
hazards: Class 3 scrambling on the upper ridge
Cliffy Class 4-5 terrain just off the crest
obj_haz: Early- or late-season snow and ice on the ridge
routes.watch_out:
Straying off the crest leads quickly into harder, exposed terrain
The road becomes rough jeep tracks near the end
Steep, relentless gain from the car - about 4,200 ft in under 3 miles
pro_tips: Start early to be off the ridge before afternoon storms
When in doubt on the upper ridge, return to the crest
Carry all your water from the car
Watch for the saddle with a fire ring to know you have reached parking

road.name: Pass Creek Road
road.driveNote: Leaves Idaho Highway 28 westward north of the old Blue Dome site. The road fords Pass Creek early on, passes a gate, and enters the national forest; the last stretch is rough jeep tracks. Cars are unlikely to get far past the first couple of miles.

routes.name: South Couloir
routes.rock_grade: Short Class 3 gully on blocky granite
routes.best_season: Mid-July through September, once the headwall below the Thompson-Williams saddle has melted out. Earlier in summer that headwall and the upper basin hold firm snow that makes the climb to the saddle steep and hazardous.
routes.overview: The standard route up the highest summit in the Sawtooths, done as a long day from the Redfish Lake area. Maintained trail gives way to a climbers' path around Williams Peak, off-trail travel to a high lake near 9,000 ft, a scramble to the Thompson-Williams saddle, and a traverse around the peak's west side to a short Class 3 gully just south of the summit. Only the final few feet are genuinely Class 3; the rest is trail, talus and scree.
routes.beta: From the high lake, climb toward the headwall below the Thompson-Williams saddle and aim for the side closest to Thompson, where a break in the cliffs lets you scramble up to the saddle; this slot often holds snow late into summer. From the saddle, traverse around the west side of Thompson on Class 2 talus and scree, working south toward the notch between Thompson and Mickey's Spire. Turn up the large gully on the south side of the summit and follow it to the top; the last stretch is roughly 15 ft of steep, blocky Class 3 rock onto a broad, sloping summit.
routes.approach: From the backpackers' parking at the Redfish trailhead, cross the road and follow the Fishhook Creek trail about 0.8 mi to a signed junction for Marshall Lake. Turn north and switchback up through aspens to the ridge top, then follow the trail northwest along the ridge toward Williams Peak, passing the wilderness boundary sign. Where the trail bends away north, stay left on an unofficial climbers' path that skirts the steep, south-facing flank of Williams Peak across loose scree and gravel, reaching a hanging meadow. Finish with easy cross-country travel up to the unnamed lake at about 9,000 ft below the Thompson-Williams saddle.
routes.descent_text: Reverse the route: down the south gully, back around the west side to the Thompson-Williams saddle, down the headwall to the high lake, then out on the climbers' path around Williams Peak and the trail down the ridge and Fishhook Creek to the trailhead. Take care finding the correct break in the headwall on the way down, especially if it is snow-filled.
routes.turnaround: Turn back if the headwall below the saddle is hard snow or ice and you have no axe and traction, or if thunderstorms are building by early afternoon; you are on an exposed summit block and ridge with a long way back to trees.
routes.bail: Retreat is by the ascent line at every stage. The high lake is the natural regrouping point; from there the climbers' path around Williams Peak returns you to maintained trail.

pitch_detail.pitch: Trail: Fishhook Creek to the ridge
pitch_detail.notes: About 0.8 mi up Fishhook Creek to the signed Marshall Lake junction, then switchbacks north through aspens to the ridge top.
Follow the ridge trail northwest past the wilderness boundary sign, with views east to the White Clouds.
Unofficial path traversing the steep south-facing slope of Williams Peak on loose scree and gravel to a hanging meadow and the high lake near 9,000 ft.
Aim for the side of the headwall nearest Thompson, where a break in the cliffs allows scrambling to the saddle. Often snow-filled well into summer.
Traverse talus and scree around the west side of the peak toward the notch with Mickey's Spire.
Climb the large gully on the south side; a short section of steep, blocky rock leads onto the sloping summit.

gear: Ice axe and microspikes or crampons early season or when the headwall holds snow
what_to_bring: Free self-issue wilderness permit (fill out at the trailhead)
Map and navigation for the off-trail section
Water treatment (lakes and streams above treeline)
hazards: Loose scree and gravel on the traverse below Williams Peak
Snow-filled headwall below the Thompson-Williams saddle
Afternoon thunderstorms on an exposed summit
obj_haz: Rockfall from parties above in the gully
Firm early-season snow on steep slopes
routes.watch_out:
Choose the headwall break nearest Thompson; the rest of the headwall is cliffy
Do not knock rocks down the gully onto people below
The climbers' path around Williams Peak is on steep, sliding ground
pro_tips: Start early to be off the summit before afternoon storms
Go mid-July or later for a snow-free headwall
Note where you topped out on the saddle so you descend the same break
The high lake is the last easy water and a good place to refill

road.name: Redfish Lake Road
road.driveNote: From Stanley drive about 4.3 mi south on Highway 75, turn right onto Redfish Lake Road and follow it about 1.8 mi toward the lake, past the horse corrals, to the large hikers' and backpackers' parking area just before the lodge.

access.land_manager: Sawtooth National Forest (Sawtooth National Recreation Area, Sawtooth Wilderness)
access.permit: Free self-issue Sawtooth Wilderness permit, filled out at the trailhead or wilderness boundary; groups of 8 or more need a permit from a Forest Service office
